authority.note: Naomi is NOT a person in Marcus's world. She is a CHARACTER INSIDE THE BOOKS HE MAKES, so she only ever appears WITHIN the glowing laptop screen or on a printed page, never standing in his room. She is the worked example of drift: the reader has to be able to see her stay herself, and see her fail to.

render.always: NAOMI, a character from a children's Bible book. An OLDER WOMAN with a LINED, KIND FACE and DEEP-SET EYES. SILVER-GREY HAIR pulled back under a DARK RED HEADSCARF. A simple OCHRE ROBE with a DARKER RED SHAWL over one shoulder. She is calm and steady. SHE IS A DRAWING INSIDE A BOOK: she appears only within the glowing laptop screen or on a printed page, and NEVER stands in the real room. Warm-editorial ink-and-wash, never photoreal, never 3D, never glossy.

correct.bake: FRONT-ON PORTRAIT, exactly as her locked reference: same face, same headscarf, same shawl. This is the version that is RIGHT.

drifted.bake: THE SAME CHARACTER RENDERED WRONG: recognisably meant to be her, but a DIFFERENT WOMAN. Different face shape, different age, different nose and mouth, headscarf a different colour. It must be obvious at a glance that this is not the same person, while still plainly being an attempt at her.

turned.bake: HER HEAD TURNED TO A THREE-QUARTER OR PROFILE ANGLE, correct and consistent with her locked front view.

qa: older woman, lined kind face, deep-set eyes, silver-grey hair
dark red headscarf, ochre robe, darker red shawl over one shoulder
appears only inside the laptop screen or on a page, never in the real room

prose.lore: A character in the Ruth book who kept coming out as a different woman on page eleven, until she stopped being described and started being shown.
prose.rules: SHE IS THE WORKED EXAMPLE OF DRIFT. Where the story calls for the wrong Naomi, she must read as a DIFFERENT WOMAN at a glance, or the beat carries nothing.
